Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Amir, a 40-year-old paramedic, sat in the quiet confines of his car, the engine idling softly as he gripped the steering wheel. The familiar antiseptic smell of the hospital lingered in his nostrils, a scent that had once signified hope and healing but now clawed at his insides, dragging him back to that harrowing night—a night he could never forget. It was a foggy evening when his younger brother, Samir, was involved in a devastating car accident. Amir had arrived at the scene minutes after the call, his heart racing with urgency, only to find that Samir was the one lying on the pavement, motionless, his body marred by visible injuries that Amir could hardly bear to witness. The trauma of seeing his brother like that—the blood, the twisted metal, the frantic cries of bystanders—had seared itself into his mind. 

Since that night, Amir had felt a heavy shroud of darkness enveloping him. He had come to believe that he was permanently changed, that he would never again be the man he once was. Thoughts of that evening invaded his mind at the most unexpected moments, often triggered by the faintest reminders—like a news report about a traffic accident or the sight of a stranger with visible wounds. Each time he was confronted with such scenes, his heart raced, and he felt the terror of that night flood back into his consciousness, making him relive the horror with full sensory clarity. The screams echoed, the smell of blood was strong, and he could feel the panic rising in his chest as if he were right back there again.

In the months that followed, Amir developed a range of maladaptive strategies to cope with the overwhelming feelings. He found himself avoiding shifts at work, despite his commitment to his team and the community. Each time he received a call, his stomach twisted into knots, and he would make an excuse to stay home, telling himself he needed time to heal. He threw himself into household chores instead, keeping busy with tasks that required his attention, hoping to suppress the haunting memories that lurked just beneath the surface. Yet, even in these moments of distraction, the thought of Samir’s accident would pierce through, reminding him of his failure to protect his brother. This spiral of avoidance began to affect his relationship with his wife, Layla. She would often find him distant, sitting in the corner of the room, choosing seats that felt the most secure, a stark contrast to their once vibrant life together. 

Amir's nights were plagued by insomnia, often interrupted by sudden awakenings when his wife reached out to him, causing him to startle as if he were in immediate danger. He had come to dread unexpected touch, a reflex that made him feel exposed and vulnerable. During the day, he struggled to concentrate, his mind drifting to memories he couldn’t fully recall, fragments of the event lost in a fog of confusion. This inability to piece together what had happened gnawed at him, reinforcing his belief that he had failed not only Samir but also himself. 

As time passed, the weight of his guilt grew heavier. Amir felt he could no longer rely on himself, believing that he was a shadow of the capable paramedic he had once been. The notion that he had failed to protect his brother haunted him relentlessly, feeding into a cycle of shame that left him feeling isolated. He would look in the mirror and see a man changed for the worse, a man who was betraying the very calling he had devoted his life to. 

Eventually, Amir found himself at a crossroads. The coping strategies he had employed were no longer effective; they were making his world smaller and darker. He missed the camaraderie of his colleagues and the sense of purpose that came with helping others. The final straw came one evening when Layla, in a moment of frustration, urged him to seek help, reminding him of the man he used to be. It was a plea filled with love, but Amir felt a sharp stab of fear at the thought of confronting his trauma. 

Now, as he sat in his car, contemplating the journey ahead, Amir felt a fragile flicker of hope mingled with deep anxiety. He feared the process of revisiting those memories, terrified of what it might reveal about himself. Yet, he also longed to reclaim his life, to find a way back to the person he once was. Seeking help felt like a first step—a chance to break free from the chains of his past and the weight of his grief.
